name: Wendy Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for fitting me in, Wendy. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We farm 110 hectares that have been in my husband Greg's family since his grandfather: 2,000 free-range laying hens, forty beef cattle and some wheat. I collect and grade eggs first thing, then open the farm shop at nine. Greg does the cattle and the field work. Afternoons I'm doing shop orders, the staff rota for our two part-timers, and posts for the shop's page.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does technology fit into that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI every single day. It does the shop's stock orders, the rota, the egg-grading records and most of my social media posts, which saves me two hours a day easily. We opened the shop eighteen months ago on a bank loan, so the savings went into that, and we've less than a month put by. I believe in standing on your own feet, and the shop is us doing exactly that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still worth having, and anyone running a small business should use them. I'd say it on the shop's page, probably with a photo of the hens. I'd say it to the other mums at church too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing really changes for us, which means the shop loan is still the big thing. In a flat economy people still buy eggs and beef, but they won't buy the fancy jams. I'd have to keep the shop busy to keep the bank happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the shop open six days and push the Christmas turkey and beef box orders hard. I'd pay an extra hundred a month off the loan whenever there's a good month. I'd keep the AI doing the admin so I can be on the shop floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit restless. I'm better when things are moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the loan payment like each month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's about the same as our mortgage, which still makes me gulp. In a good month the shop covers it with room to spare. In a bad month Greg's cattle money tops it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Greg make of all the AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Greg calls it my robot secretary and pretends he doesn't use it. Then he asks it about the weather every morning. He's coming round.

say: The tools are **still worth having** for any small business.
I'd say it on the **shop's page** with a photo of the hens.
think: Nothing changes, so the **shop loan** is still the big thing.
In a flat economy people buy eggs but **skip the jams**.
do: Push **Christmas turkey** and beef box orders hard.
Pay an extra **hundred a month** off the loan in good months.
feel: **Fine**, a bit **restless**, better when things move.
S0.quote: In a flat economy people still buy eggs and beef, but they won't buy the fancy jams.
fieldNote: Her thin savings come from **investing in the shop**, a choice she's proud of.
Her income risk is **customers' spending**, not her own tasks.
Her husband is **slowly coming round** to AI.

steps.text: Keep the farm shop open six days a week
Pay an extra hundred a month off the shop loan
Push Christmas turkey and beef box pre-orders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is great for small businesses that move quickly, and people should learn the tools rather than wait for the government. I'd say it on the shop's page and at the parish business breakfast. I'd offer to show other farm shops what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's mostly good for me. AI takes over the thinking jobs I already hand it, and more: ordering, invoices, answering customer messages. The worry is my customers: lots of them work in offices in town. If my customers' office jobs shrink, they'll stop buying the twelve-pound steaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put in an AI ordering and checkout system for the shop, so one part-timer can run it while I'm with the hens. I'd add a cheaper 'family box' of eggs and mince for people watching their money. I'd run a paid workshop for other farm shops on using AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for my customers, quietly pleased for us. That's honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would one part-timer lose hours if you automate the till?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, Karen probably would, and that's hard because she's my neighbour. I'd try to move her onto making the ready meals instead. I wouldn't just cut her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people shouldn't wait for government. What if your customers can't find new jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the church and families would have to help, like they always have. I'd give the food bank more eggs. I don't think a cheque from the government fixes a person's pride.

say: Small businesses that **move quickly** will do well.
People should **learn the tools** rather than wait for government.
think: AI takes the **thinking jobs** I already hand it, and more.
Office **customers losing work** would stop buying twelve-pound steaks.
do: Install an **AI ordering and checkout** system.
Add a cheaper **family box** of eggs and mince.
Run a paid **AI workshop** for other farm shops.
feel: **Uneasy** for customers, **quietly pleased** for the farm.
S1.quote: If my customers' office jobs shrink, they'll stop buying the twelve-pound steaks.
fieldNote: She is **openly pleased** while worried for others.
Automating the till would cut **her neighbour Karen's** hours.
She trusts **church and family** over government cheques.

steps.text: Install an AI ordering and checkout system in the farm shop
Run paid AI workshops for other farm shop owners
Train Karen to use the new shop system and make ready meals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but people who roll up their sleeves will come through it. I'd say businesses should be free to adapt without a pile of new rules. I'd say families and churches need to look after their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, 2028 doesn't hurt the farm much; I'd be using AGI for everything on the business side. The danger is 2031, when huge robot egg farms can sell eggs for pennies. And by then half my customers might have lost their office jobs in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look at leasing an egg-collecting robot before the rush, so we're cheaper too. I'd move the shop towards things robots can't fake: our own beef, the farm story, school visits. I'd cut our own spending to the bone and pay down the loan as fast as possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. I don't freeze; I make lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jakub and Rosie?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids that hard work and faith will see us through, and that we'll all pitch in. Jakub would want to run the robot, honestly. Rosie would ask if the hens are safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a contradiction in buying a robot while your customers lose jobs to robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, there is, and I see it. But if I don't, a bigger farm will, and then we're both gone. I'd rather keep our farm and our two part-timers than be noble and broke.

say: People who **roll up their sleeves** will come through it.
Businesses should be **free to adapt** without new rules.
think: AGI in 2028 helps the business side, but **2031 robot egg farms** undercut us.
Many of my customers may already have **lost office jobs** in 2028.
do: Lease an **egg-collecting robot** before the rush.
Shift the shop to **our own beef** and school visits.
Cut spending and **pay down the loan** fast.
feel: **Anxious, but busy**, making lists rather than freezing.
S2.quote: I'd rather keep our farm and our two part-timers than be noble and broke.
fieldNote: She sees **two hits**: customers in 2028, egg prices in 2031.
She names the **contradiction** of buying a robot herself.

steps.text: Lease an egg-collecting robot for the hen houses
Cut family spending to essentials for a year
Pay down the farm shop loan as fast as possible

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair run-up and businesses can plan for it. I'd tell other farm shops to start now. I'd say it at the parish breakfast and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, robots around 2034 give me time to pay off the shop loan first. By 2031 I'd have AGI running the shop admin. I'd be able to buy rather than lease a robot by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd clear the shop loan within four years. I'd save a robot fund after that. I'd build the farm's school visits into a proper paid programme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but pleased with the chance. It's a race I can see the finish of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jakub be doing by 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jakub would be twenty-three. I'd want him to do an agricultural engineering apprenticeship. Then he could run the robots here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bird flu. Honestly, a bird flu outbreak in the hens worries me more than AGI. One bad winter and the shop has no eggs.

say: Five years is a **fair run-up**, and businesses can plan.
Other farm shops should **start now**, while there's time to do it properly.
think: Robots around 2034 give time to **pay off** the shop loan first.
I could **buy, not lease**, a robot by then.
do: Clear the shop loan **within four years**.
Save a **robot fund** once the loan is paid.
Build the farm's school visits into a **paid programme**.
S3.quote: A bird flu outbreak in the hens worries me more than AGI.
fieldNote: Five years turns robots into **an investment plan**.
Her son's **engineering apprenticeship** is part of the farm's future.
**Bird flu** is a bigger fear than AGI.

steps.text: Clear the farm shop loan within four years
Start a fund to buy a hen-house robot outright
Steer Jakub toward an agricultural engineering apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and nobody should waste it. I'd say families should prepare their kids. I'd keep posting about how we use AI in the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots in 2039 means the shop loan is long gone and the kids are grown. With ten years, we could plan robots the way you'd plan a new barn. It's the best version for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on growing the shop. I'd add a café in a few years. I'd make sure Rosie and Jakub know the farm is theirs if they want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. The ordinary worries stay, but they're the kind I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop loan for the first few years, and bird flu, always. And whether the town keeps its office jobs till 2036. That's where my customers come from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want Rosie to farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosie wants to be a vet. I'd be proud either way. I'd tell her to do what she loves and work hard at it.

say: Ten years is **a gift** nobody should waste.
Families should **prepare their kids** in good time.
I'll keep posting how we use **AI in the shop**.
think: Robots in 2039 come after the **loan is gone** and the kids are grown.
We could plan robots **like a new barn**.
do: Add a **café** in a few years.
Tell the kids the farm is **theirs if they want** it.
S4.quote: With ten years, we could plan robots the way you'd plan a new barn.
fieldNote: Ten years makes this the **best version** for her.
Her worries return to **bird flu** and the loan.
She sees robots as a **planned investment** like a barn.

steps.text: Keep growing the farm shop and box orders
Add a café to the farm shop in a few years
Offer Jakub and Rosie the farm if they want it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my customers would lose their office jobs first and then robot egg farms would undercut us, all while we still owe on the shop. What would help is fair leasing for small farms, so we're not shut out of robots. And the bank giving us time on the loan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask why people come to a farm shop. They don't come for cheap eggs; they come to see the hens and talk to someone. Nobody drives twenty minutes to chat with a robot about the weather.

headlineQuote: Nobody drives twenty minutes to chat with a robot about the weather.
portrait: Wendy, 43, runs a **farm shop** on her husband's family mixed farm with 2,000 laying hens.
She uses AI **every day** for orders, rotas and posts, and opened the shop on a bank loan.
A churchgoer who prefers **self-reliance** to government help, she still protects her part-time staff.
Her risk comes through **customers' office jobs** and cheap robot eggs, not her own tasks.
She's **anxious** only in the fast world and sees long timelines as a planned investment.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because customers lose office jobs and robot egg farms undercut her.
whatWouldHelp: **Fair leasing** for small farms and more time on the shop loan.
